desc:
You are given a text s and a list of words that all have the same length wordLen. The list is passed as a single string words: the words written one after another with no separators, so the i-th word is words[i * wordLen .. (i + 1) * wordLen). Words may repeat.

A substring of s is a full concatenation if it can be cut into consecutive pieces of length wordLen that are exactly the given words, each word used as many times as it appears in the list, in any order. Return all start indices of full concatenations in increasing order (an empty array if there are none).

s = "barfoothefoobarman", words = "foobar", wordLen = 3   (words: foo, bar)
"barfoo" at 0 and "foobar" at 9
result = [0, 9]
s = "wordgoodgoodgoodbestword", words = "goodgoodbestword", wordLen = 4
words: good, good, best, word; only the substring at 8 matches
result = [8]
constraints: wordLen ≤ words.length ≤ 5,000 and words.length is a multiple of wordLen
s and words consist of lowercase English letters
hints: Let total = (number of words) * wordLen. Every candidate substring has length total, so there are n - total + 1 of them. Checking each one by cutting it into words is correct but slow when there are many words.
A match must be aligned on word boundaries relative to its start. So handle each starting offset 0 .. wordLen - 1 separately and jump through the text in steps of wordLen.

For each offset, slide a window of whole words with a hash map of word counts. When a word occurs too often, move the left edge forward word by word; when a word is not in the list at all, restart after it. A window containing exactly the right number of words is a match.
editorial: Brute force would cut each of up to n candidate substrings into k words and compare counts, O(n · k · wordLen). Instead, note that all words have the same length, so for a fixed offset o the text splits into the aligned pieces s[o..o+L), s[o+L..o+2L), ... and a match is a run of exactly k consecutive pieces that form the required multiset. Doing this for each of the L = wordLen offsets covers every possible start.

For one offset, move a right pointer one piece at a time and keep the counts of pieces in the window. If the new piece is not in the word list, nothing containing it can match, so clear the window and restart after it. If its count exceeds the allowed count, advance the left pointer (dropping pieces) until the count is fine again. When the window holds k pieces it is a match: record the left index, and drop the leftmost piece so the window can continue. Each piece is added and removed at most once per offset, so the total work is O(n) piece operations per offset: O(n · wordLen) character work for slicing, about 240,000 here. Sort the collected indices at the end.
